evidence_text: The commission concluded that canopy loss is a public health problem before it is an aesthetic one. Its recommendations, however, were modest. full_cite: Quenby 25 (Harlan Quenby, invented historian, The Invented Book of Water Rights, Fictional University Press, 2025, p. 14)
evidence_text: Every allocation regime eventually meets a drought it was not written for. The riparian doctrine assumed that a river's flow would be shared among the landholders along its banks, and it worked tolerably well so long as the river kept flowing. When the Castellan basin lost a third of its average discharge over a decade, the doctrine offered no rule for deciding whose share should shrink first. Courts improvised. Some ordered proportional cuts, others protected the oldest farms, and a few simply declined to rule until the legislature acted. The result was a patchwork in which two neighbouring farms on the same tributary could face entirely different obligations depending on which county courthouse they happened to be closer to.

evidence_text: The result was a patchwork in which two neighbouring farms on the same tributary could face entirely different obligations depending on which county courthouse they happened to be closer to. The legislature, when it finally acted, did not resolve the patchwork so much as freeze it. Its statute confirmed every allocation that a court had already ordered and applied proportional cuts only to rights that had never been litigated. Farmers who had sued early kept their water; farmers who had trusted their neighbours lost it. The lesson is not that litigation was rewarded but that the rules of the drought were written by whoever happened to be in court first, and that later reformers inherited those rules as though they had been chosen.

tag: Automation intensifies work rather than replacing it
full_cite: Thorne 26 (Beatrix Thorne, invented labour economist, "Measured Tasks," Fictional Brightwell Institute Working Paper 12, 2026)
evidence_text: Automation rarely eliminates a job outright; it removes the tasks within a job that were easiest to measure. In the warehouses the Brightwell Institute studied, scanning and routing software took over the counting that pickers used to do by hand, and managers responded not by cutting staff but by raising the number of orders each picker was expected to fill per hour. Injury reports rose in the eighteen months after installation, concentrated in the lower back and wrists, and turnover among new hires nearly doubled. The institute's interviews suggest that workers experienced the software less as a tool than as a supervisor that never left the floor. Productivity, measured as orders per labour hour, improved by eleven percent, but the institute estimates that the costs of recruitment and injury absorbed most of that gain within two years.

full_cite: Marchetti 26 (Ines Marchetti, invented law professor, "Retreat by Definition," Fictional Coastal Law Journal, 2026)
evidence_text: The Coastal Resilience Act defines a managed retreat as "the planned, voluntary relocation of residents and public infrastructure away from areas of recurring flood loss, financed in whole or in part by public funds." Read literally, that definition excludes almost every buyout program now operating, because most of them purchase single homes after a flood rather than planning the relocation of a neighbourhood before one. The distinction matters for funding. Programs that fit the statutory definition qualify for the federal match; programs that do not must rely on state bond money, which in most coastal states has already been committed to seawalls. The practical effect is that the definition written to encourage retreat instead channels money toward the defenses that retreat was meant to replace.

tag: Voluntary retreat lets one holdout stall a street
full_cite: Oyelaran 25 (Tomi Oyelaran, invented policy analyst, Fictional Housing Quarterly, 2025)
evidence_text: The Coastal Resilience Act defines a managed retreat as "the planned, voluntary relocation of residents and public infrastructure away from areas of recurring flood loss, financed in whole or in part by public funds." Its drafters meant the word voluntary to protect homeowners, but in practice it has protected the program's budget. Because no resident can be required to leave, agencies can decline to fund a relocation until every household on a street has agreed, and a single holdout can stall a project for years. Interviews with program staff in three states describe streets where most residents wanted to leave and none could, because the buyout offer was contingent on a unanimity the statute never demanded but never forbade.
